CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 1 Two children observing a beetle, seedling and ripples in a puddle. 
 Look around you right now. Something is happening everywhere you turn.  
 A fan is spinning. Sunlight is falling through a window and landing in a bright patch on the floor. Somewhere nearby, water is boiling, or a bird is calling, or dust is drifting through a beam of light. None of this is unusual. All of it is worth a second look.  
 1.1 What Is Science? 
 You have been noticing things like this your whole life — why the moon seems to follow the car, why ice feels wet, why your shadow stretches long in the evening. Those questions were not childish. They were the beginning of something.  
 Now you are ready to go further.  
 An ordinary event can become a scientific question when you look closely.  
 Science is not a pile of facts to memorise. Science is a way of working. It means observing carefully, asking sharp questions, testing what you think you know, and being willing to change your mind when the evidence says you should.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 2 Science Is Not Kept in a Building 
 Science does not live in laboratories. Laboratories are useful, but science is wherever something is happening.  
 It is in the kitchen, where heat turns a soft batter into a firm, holey dosa. It is on the cricket field, where a ball bends in the air because of the way it was spun. It is in the soil under a mango tree, where organisms too small to see are breaking down fallen leaves. It is inside your own body, where your heart is beating right now without being told to.  A dosa cooking in a pan. 
 An Unfinished Map 
 Here is something surprising: science is not finished.  
 Think of what we know as a map of a huge, mostly unexplored land. Some regions are surveyed in fine detail. Others are sketched roughly. Some are still blank. And every time explorers map a new region, its edges open onto territory nobody knew existed. The map does not shrink the unknown — it reveals more of it.  An unfinished map and pencil. 
 Sometimes the mapmakers get it wrong. For centuries people were certain the Sun travelled around the Earth, because that is exactly what it looks like. Careful observation showed otherwise, and the map had to be redrawn. That correction was not a failure of science. It was science working as it should.  
 The Most Important Tool 
 You will use many instruments in this book — thermometers, magnets, lenses, balances. But the tool that matters most is not one you can hold. It is  curiosity .  
 Curiosity is what makes you look up at a night sky and wonder what the stars actually are, and how far away. It is what makes you notice that a flower on your balcony is shut at dawn and open by mid-morning, and then wonder how it knows.  An open flower and a closed bud.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 3 Think It Through Why might this happen? A flower has no eyes and no clock. What could it be responding to? You do not need the right answer yet — only a reasonable guess. A possible explanation is a  hypothesis . A  prediction  states what you expect to observe if it is right. For example, if light triggers opening, what should happen when the plant is shaded?  
 One Idea in Many Places 
 Some of what you learn in this book will be useful the same week you learn it. You will understand why food spoils faster in May than in December, why a frayed electrical wire is dangerous, how boiling kills many disease-causing microbes in water, while leaving dissolved chemical contaminants behind.  
 But the real reward comes later, and it is stranger than that.  
 Leave a wet shirt on a line and by evening it is dry. Pour water into an earthen  matka  and the water inside stays cool even on a hot afternoon. Watch the sky before the monsoon and see clouds thickening where there was clear blue an hour ago.  
 Three ordinary things. They seem to have nothing to do with each other.  
 Two involve evaporation directly; cloud formation needs another change as well.  
 Drying Drying Cooling Cooling Cloud forming Cloud forming 
 In all three, water is leaving a liquid surface and moving into the air as an invisible vapour. That is what dries the shirt. That is what cools the  matka  — water seeping through the clay escapes from its surface and carries warmth away with it. Evaporation supplies water vapour. Clouds become visible when vapour cools and condenses into droplets or forms ice crystals; vapour itself is invisible.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 4 Think It Through Can you explain why? If evaporation cools the  matka , what does that suggest about why you feel cold when you step out of a swimming pool into the wind?  
 Evaporation connects the shirt and the pot. Cloud formation also requires condensation or ice formation. Name each change rather than treating every water process as the same event.  
 Clouds become visible when cooling water vapour condenses into tiny droplets or forms ice crystals. Evaporation supplies the vapour; condensation helps form clouds.  
 A shared explanation can connect observations; check where it works and where another process is needed.  
 1.2 What This Book Will Ask You 
 Begin with the Earth — as far as we know, the only place in the universe where anything is alive.  
 A seedling, food, water, everyday materials and the Moon. 
 A seed pushes a pale shoot up through dark soil. A caterpillar seals itself away and comes out with wings. A calf that could barely stand in the morning is running across the field by the end of the month. Growing is so ordinary that we stop noticing it happening. But how does a plant build an entire body out of soil, water and air?  
 Living things need materials and energy to grow. Green plants make sugars using light, water and carbon dioxide; animals obtain food by eating. In a country this large, that alone is a huge subject — pongal in one state, litti in another, a fish curry along the coast, a plate of rajma somewhere north. What are these dishes actually made of? And how could you find out for yourself, instead of being told?

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 5 Then there is water. You have jumped into a puddle after rain. But where was that water an hour before it fell on you, and how did it get up there? Cool it and it turns to ice. Heat it and it leaves as steam. What is going on?  
 And how hot is hot? When someone in your house has a fever, nobody wants a guess. They want a number.  
 Now look at what things are made of — paper, the metal of a key, a plastic scale, a rubber eraser, the magnet holding a cupboard shut, the cloth of your shirt. Each one was chosen for a reason. Could a key be made of rubber? Why not?  
 And when the Earth runs out of questions, there is the sky above it.  
 These questions connect different parts of science. Following water leads from a puddle to the weather. Studying a plant leads to light, air and food. Comparing materials leads to the design of useful objects. Look for these connections as you read. Ask what changes something, and what evidence could help explain it.  
 Every one of these has an answer. Not all of them are in this book.  
 1.3 Asking and Testing Questions 
 You already do science. You have simply never called it that.  
 Suppose the clock on your wall has stopped. Both hands are frozen at ten past four.  
 The first thing you do is ask a question, even if only in your head:  why   has   it   stopped?   
 Clock hands touching and a replacement cell. Hands touching Cell 
 Then, almost without noticing, you make a guess. The cell inside must be finished.  
 Making a guess is the easy part. What matters is what you do next. You take the clock down, open the back, and fit a new cell.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 6 If the hands begin to move, a used-up cell is one explanation. Refitting the cell also changed its contact with the terminals, so that observation alone does not prove which change mattered.  
 But suppose they do not move.  
 Now stop and notice something. The clock is still stopped, so it feels as though nothing has been achieved. That is not true. A failed replacement narrows the possibilities only if the new cell works, faces the right way and makes contact. Check these before ruling out the cell as a cause.  
 So you make a second guess. Perhaps the cell is fine but is not pressing properly against the metal contacts. You push it in firmly and give it a moment. Still nothing.  
 A third guess, then: something inside is stuck. You look more closely and find the thin second hand has caught against the minute hand and cannot pass it.  
 Question. Guess. Test. Look honestly at what happened. Guess again if you must.  
 Nobody sat you down and taught you that sequence. Yet it is very close to what a scientist does when facing something no one has ever explained.  
 The Steps Behind It 
 What you did with the clock has a name. It is called the  scientific   method , and written out plainly it looks like this:  
 1. Observe something that puzzles you or catches your interest.  
 2. Ask a question about it.  Instruments for measuring time. Instruments for measuring time.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 7 3. Guess a possible answer.  
 4. Test the guess, through an experiment or through further careful observation.  
 5. Examine the result and decide whether it actually answers your question.  
 That list looks tidier than real life ever is. Very often you finish step five only to discover you are back at step three with a fresh guess. Sometimes the test throws up something you were not even looking for, and that becomes a better question than the one you started with.  
 This is one useful route through an investigation, not a compulsory order for every kind of science. What matters is that the guess comes  before  the test, and that you accept the result even when it is not the one you wanted.  
 Observe Question Guess Test Examine result 
 An observation describes what you notice: the clock hands have not moved. An explanation suggests a reason: the cell may be used up. Keeping these separate helps you test your idea honestly.  
 For a fair comparison, change one thing while keeping other conditions similar. If you replace the cell and free the hands together, you will not know which change mattered. Repeating a check can help you spot a result that happened only by chance.  Instruments for measuring time. Instruments for measuring time.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 8 Think It Through Write about a problem you worked out for yourself recently. It does not have to be a science problem. List the steps you took, in order. Was there a point where you had to change your first guess?  
 Everyone Does This 
 Scientists follow the scientific method for a living. But nobody owns it, and it is used every day by people who would never call themselves scientists.  
 A cook lifts the lid off the idli batter in the morning and finds it flat instead of risen. She asks why. Was the kitchen too cold overnight? Was the batter ground too thin? She will not solve it by worrying — she will change one thing tomorrow and watch what happens.  Cook inspecting batter 
 A tailor's machine starts skipping stitches. He does not replace the whole machine. He checks the needle first, then the thread tension, then the bobbin — one at a time, because changing everything at once would tell him nothing.  Tailor checking a needle 
 An electrician is called about a tubelight that flickers for a long time before it steadies. Is it the tube, the starter, or the wiring? Each of those can be tested separately.  Electrician checking a disconnected fitting 
 None of them are in a laboratory. All of them are doing exactly what step three and step four describe: guess, then test — and crucially, test  one   thing   at   a   time , so that the result actually means something.  
 A useful record is specific. Describe which part of a puddle’s edge moved and when. A sketch can preserve details that memory loses. Keep what you observed separate from your explanation of why it happened.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 9 Investigate Choose one thing near your home that changes over time — a plant on a windowsill, a puddle after rain, ants around a spill, the shadow of a pole.  1. Watch it for five minutes without doing anything to it.  2. Write down three things you actually saw. Not what you think should happen — what happened.  3. Write one question your observation raised.  
 1.4 Curiosity, Company and a Long Road 
 Everything in this chapter rests on one habit, and it is not a difficult one. Notice things.  
 Noticing sounds too simple to matter. It is not. Most people walk past a hundred small oddities a day without registering a single one. The person who stops and says  hold   on,   that's   strange  has done the hardest part already. Everything else — the questions, the guesses, the tests — follows from that pause.  
 And you do not have to do any of it alone. Science has a reputation for lonely geniuses, and it is mostly wrong. Discoveries today come from teams, often spread across many countries, arguing with one another and checking each other's work. Being told you are wrong by someone who has looked carefully at your evidence is not an insult. It is one of the most useful things that can happen to you.  Instruments for measuring time. Instruments for measuring time.

CHAPTER 1 The Wonderful World of Science LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 10 So when you are stuck, ask someone. Compare what you saw with what your friend saw. If you disagree about what happened, that disagreement is worth more than either of your answers.  
 One last thing, and it is important. You will not find the answers to all your questions this year. Some of what you wonder about in Grade 6 you will only understand in Grade 9, or later, or possibly never — because nobody has worked it out yet.  
 That is not a warning. It is the best part.  
 Describe an event separately from a friend, then compare your accounts. Did you notice the same details? Which statements describe what you saw, and which suggest a reason? Differences give you something to check together. Finding an answer may need longer observation, a better comparison, or a more precise question.  
 Think It Through Write down one Why? question about something you have noticed but never had explained. How might you begin to find the answer? Who could you ask, and what could you test?  
 Science begins with noticing. It continues with asking. And it never quite ends.  A folded paper plane. A folded paper plane.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 1 Living things in a schoolyard 
 Go outside your classroom. Stand still for two minutes.  
 Look for grass in a crack, insects near a wall, or birds overhead. Choose two plants. Compare their leaves. What differences can you describe?  
 A planted tree and a plant growing without anyone sowing it both belong in your record. You do not need to know how something arrived before you can observe it.  
 This chapter is about that variety. How much of it is there? How do we make sense of it? And why are the living things in one place so different from the living things in another?  
 2.1 The Variety Around Us  
 A quick glance may tell you that a tree is there. A closer look can reveal the shape of its leaves, where its branches begin, or insects on its bark. Listening may reveal a bird you cannot see.  
 Looking carefully is a skill. Like any skill, it gets better with practice.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 2 Practise looking closely in the investigation below. Tables 2.1 and 2.2 show possible records; your own entries may be different.  
 Investigate You will need: a notebook, a pencil, a water bottle.  1. Before the visit, copy the headings of Tables 2.1 and 2.2 into your notebook. Leave room for your own rows.  2. With your teacher, spend one period in a garden, park or school ground. Record the place, date and time.  3. Walk slowly, then stop at a safe place. Stand still and listen for thirty seconds. What different sounds can you hear?  4. Add a row for each kind of plant or animal you observe. If you do not know its name, describe or sketch it. For example: "small plant, three leaves together, near the tap".  5. Record only what you can establish. Write "not seen" for a feature you looked for but did not see. Do not pluck leaves or flowers or disturb animals.  Compare your records with a partner. Which living things were difficult to find or describe? What made them difficult?  Safety: Stay with your group. Do not touch any animal. Do not put your fingers into holes or under stones.  Animal feet. Animal feet.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 3 In these two example tables, a dash means that a feature was not recorded. It does not mean the feature is absent. A plant without flowers today may flower in another season.  
 Table 2.1 · Example plant records Name / description  Stem  Leaves  Flowers  Anything else  Common grass  Soft and thin  One thin leaf at a time  —  Grows in a thick patch  Tulsi  Hard and thin  Leaves in pairs, facing each other  Small, pinkish purple  Smells strong when rubbed  Hibiscus  Hard and woody  Broad leaves with toothed edges  Red flower  —  
 Grass                         Tulsi                         Hibiscus Grass Tulsi Hibiscus 
 Read across a row to connect a plant with its features. Then read down a column to compare that feature across plants. Which differences would be hardest to show in a drawing?

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 4 The pictures show the three plants named in Table 2.1. They are enlarged by different amounts so you can see their features; do not use their printed heights to compare their actual sizes.  
 Were any two plants in your record alike in every feature you recorded? Would that prove they were the same kind of plant? What else could you examine?  
 Table 2.2 · Example animal records Name / description  Where you saw it  Doing / eating  How it moved  Anything else  Crow  On a wall, then a tree  Pecking at something  Walks, then flies  Carried a twig away  Ant  Along the edge of a step  Carrying a crumb  Walks  Six legs; followed the ant in front  
 A moving animal may disappear before you finish recording it. Try watching from one place as well as walking slowly. Which method helped you find which animals?  
 Separate what you saw from what you infer. The crow was seen on a wall and in a tree; that does not tell us every place it lives. "Pecking at something" does not identify its food. What further observation could help?  
 The variety of living things found in one region is called its  biodiversity .  
 Your school ground has its own biodiversity. So does a pond. So does a forest, a seashore, and even the soil in a flowerpot.  Different forms of plants. Different forms of plants.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 5 Think It Through Your search lasted one period. Name two kinds of living things that your method might have missed. Plan one change to the time, place or method that could help you find them.  
 Living Things Need Each Other  
 The living things in a place are not just sharing space. They are joined to each other.  
 A tree can provide shade for smaller plants and nesting places for birds. Some birds feed on insects on its bark. A fruit-eating bird may carry a seed away; the seed can grow if it reaches suitable conditions. Fallen leaves provide food for decomposers, which help return nutrients to the soil.  
 Removing a tree can remove shade, nest sites and a source of fallen leaves. The effects depend on which organisms use it and what other resources are available nearby.  
 Choose one plant or animal from your own record. Draw it in the centre of a notebook page. Add other living things it may depend on, or that may depend on it. Use arrows labelled "food", "shelter" or another relationship. Mark each link as observed, read about, or still a guess. Compare your diagram with a partner. Choose one uncertain link and suggest how you could check it. If one organism disappeared from your diagram, which links would be affected? Could another organism supply the same resource? Explain what you know and what you would need to find out.  Different forms of plants. Different forms of plants.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 6 2.2 Making Sense of the Variety  
 Your records may contain many kinds of living things. Grouping them can help you compare a feature without searching through every entry.  
 In a stationery shop, keeping pens together helps a customer find a pen. Arranging goods by price answers a different question: what can I buy with this amount of money?  
 Scientists do the same with living things. Putting things into groups by the features they share is called  grouping .  
 Investigate You will need: old magazines or newspapers, scissors, glue, small cards.  1. Cut out pictures of plants and animals. Paste one on each card. Try to make at least thirty cards in the class.  2. Work in groups of five or six. Put all your cards together.  3. Sort the pile into groups. You decide what the groups will be.  4. Write down, in one line, the rule you used.  5. Now mix all the cards again. Sort them a second time, using a completely different rule.  Compare both your sortings with another group's.  Did any two groups in the class use the same rule?  Safety: Use scissors carefully, with your teacher’s guidance.  Seeds for comparing features. Seeds for comparing features.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 7 A Grouping Needs a Clear Rule  
 Take one sorted group and check every card against its rule. Two different rules can both be useful, but a card can still be placed incorrectly.  
 Different groups may use size, food or surroundings. Check what the pictures actually show before using these features.  
 Some ways of grouping:  Flowers · Stem · Food · Habitat 
 Choose a rule to suit your question, then apply it consistently. If a picture does not show the feature you need, mark it "not enough information". A picture without a visible flower does not prove that the plant never flowers.  
 A gardener comparing shade might group plants by height. Someone studying their flowers would need a different grouping. Explain what your rule helps you find out and what it leaves out.  
 Scientists also study groups whose members share several inherited features. Knowing one feature can then help us predict others. Later in this chapter, you will test such a connection.  
 How would a library arranged by book size help a reader? What would be harder to find?  
 2.2.1 Grouping Plants  
 Look at Table 2.1 again. The features you wrote there — stem, leaves, flowers — are the same features we can use to sort plants.  
 Begin with stems: their firmness, whether they are woody, and where they branch. Examine plants your teacher says are safe to handle.  Different forms of plants. Different forms of plants.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 8 Investigate 1. Go out to the same place as before. Choose six plants of clearly different sizes.  2. Stand next to each one. Is it shorter than you, about your height, or taller?  3. Look at the stem near the ground. Is it green or brown?  4. Bend the stem very gently with one finger. Does it bend, or is it stiff? Stop as soon as you feel it resist. A broken stem can kill the plant.  5. See where the branches start. Near the ground, or higher up?  6. Record these features using the headings in Table 2.3. Group your plants by shared stem features and explain your rule.  Did height and stem features give you the same groups? Which plants were difficult to place?  
 Table 2.3 · Grouping plants by height and stem Plant  Height compared with you  Stem colour  Stem texture  Branching  Mango  Taller  Brown  Hard  High  Rose  About the same  Brown  Hard  Low  Tomato  Shorter  Green  Soft  Low  Different forms of plants. Different forms of plants.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 9 Herbs, Shrubs and Trees  
 Compare your records with the descriptions below. Your sample may not contain all three forms, and young or pruned plants may be harder to classify.  
 Mango · tree Rose · shrub Tomato · herb 
 Compare stems and branching Trees Shrubs Herbs Trees  are woody plants that usually develop a main trunk supporting a crown of branches. Mango is an example. A young mango is still a tree even when it is shorter than a mature tomato plant.  Shrubs  are woody plants that usually branch close to the ground, often with several main stems. A rose bush is an example. Observe the branching as well as the height.  Plants with soft, non-woody stems are called  herbs . Many are small, such as mint, coriander and tomato, but height alone does not define a herb.  
 Woody stems support branches and can thicken as a plant grows. Look at the base of a tree and then a herb: what differences can you describe without damaging either?  
 A banana plant is a large herb. Its trunk-like structure is a  pseudostem , made from tightly overlapping leaf bases rather than a woody trunk. Its height does not make it a tree.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 10 Plants That Cannot Stand Up  
 Not every plant can hold itself up.  
 Climber · grape vine Creeper · pumpkin 
 Compare growth habits Climbers Creepers Some plants have stems that are too weak to stand. So they climb up something else — a wall, a fence, a stick, or another plant. These are called  climbers . A money plant is a climber. So is a grape vine.  Other plants also have weak stems. But instead of climbing, they spread flat along the ground. These are called  creepers . Pumpkin and watermelon plants are creepers.  
 Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, not a separate woody/non-woody division. A grape vine is a woody climber; a pumpkin has non-woody trailing stems. A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.  
 A climber and a creeper both have stems that need support or spread along the ground. What observations would you need before deciding which receives more light?  
 So far you have grouped plants using only the stem. Leaves give us another way to sort the same plants. We can compare these groups with the stem groups.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 11 Lines on a Leaf  
 Hold a leaf up against the light. You will see thin lines running through it. These lines are  veins . The pattern the veins make is called  venation .  
 Veins contain tissues that transport water and dissolved substances. They carry water into the leaf and sugars made in the leaf to other parts of the plant. They also help support the leaf.  
 Investigate You will need: fallen leaves of at least four different plants, thin paper, a pencil with soft lead.  1. Put a leaf on the desk with its back side facing up. The veins stand out more on that side.  2. Place a sheet of thin paper over the leaf.  3. Hold the paper still. Rub the side of the pencil lead flat across it, using light strokes.  4. Check the print against the leaf. If the veins are unclear, adjust the paper or pressure and try again.  5. Do this for every leaf. Write the plant's name next to each print.  Put all your prints side by side.  Group the prints by their vein patterns. How many groups does your sample support? Explain your rule. If all the patterns look alike, compare with another group’s leaves.  
 A rubbing is a record made by a method. A faint patch may mean the paper moved or the pencil missed it. Check that patch on the actual leaf before describing its veins. Keep an unclear print beside your improved one so you can explain why you changed the record.  Leaf veins. Leaf veins.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 12 Compare the vein pattern separately from the leaf outline. Two leaves can have different outlines yet share a vein pattern. Point to the lines that support your grouping; another group should be able to follow your rule without knowing the plant names.  
 Two Patterns  
 Compare your prints with these examples. Two common patterns are shown here; your sample may contain only one.  
 Hibiscus · reticulate Banana · parallel Grass · parallel 
 Compare vein patterns Reticulate venation Parallel venation In  reticulate   venation , veins branch to form a net. A thick middle vein is visible in the hibiscus leaf; finer veins branch and join around it. Mango, neem and peepal also have net-like venation.  In other leaves, many veins run alongside one another. This pattern is called  parallel   venation . In a grass blade they run along the length of the leaf. A banana leaf has a strong middle vein, with many parallel side veins running out towards its edges. Parallel venation does not mean that a leaf has no middle vein.  
 These two patterns help you compare many of the leaves around you. Look closely: real leaves sometimes show exceptions.  
 Predict the venation of wheat or maize from the examples. Then inspect a leaf or a clear photograph. Was your prediction supported? Leaf shape alone is not proof of its vein pattern.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 13 Leaves are only part of the comparison. Next, examine roots.  
 Under the Ground  
 Roots hold plants in place and take up water and dissolved minerals. You can observe their growth as seeds germinate.  
 Investigate You will need: a handful of chana (chickpea) seeds, a handful of wheat seeds, two shallow trays or plates, cotton cloth or cotton wool, water.  1. Soak both kinds of seed in water overnight.  2. Spread a wet cloth in each tray. Put the chana seeds in one tray. Put the wheat seeds in the other.  3. Keep both trays in the same place. Keep the cloth damp, not flooded, and check it every morning for six days.  4. From day three, inspect the seedlings daily. Record when each germinates and sketch the roots without tearing them.  5. On day six, compare several seedlings of each kind. Keep any that germinated late and observe them for a few more days. Do not pull roots out of the cloth; examine them gently.  Draw what grew from each kind of seed in your notebook. Use the same scale for both drawings.  Could drawings alone tell you which plant is harder to pull out? What would you need to keep alike in a comparison of root anchorage?  
 Give each seedling a small identifying label and date each sketch. This lets you follow one seedling through time instead of mistaking differences between seedlings for changes in one plant. Place a ruler beside it without disturbing the roots; include a scale in your drawing.  Leaf veins. Leaf veins.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 14 Count age from germination as well as recording the calendar date. If one seed germinated on Monday and another on Thursday, drawings made on Friday show different stages of growth. Compare seedlings of similar age before deciding that a difference belongs to the two kinds of plant.  
 Two Kinds of Root  
 Compare several seedlings of each kind. Did they germinate at the same time? Root systems change as seedlings develop, so record the age as well as the shape.  
 Chana · taproot Wheat · fibrous roots 
 Compare root systems Taproot system Fibrous root system A chana seedling usually develops one main root with smaller side roots. A main root of this kind is a  taproot . Mustard and radish also develop taproots. The enlarged edible part of a radish includes a swollen taproot that stores food.  As the wheat seedling develops, several thin roots appear. Later, more roots grow from the base of the stem, forming a spreading bunch without one dominant main root. These are called  fibrous   roots . Grass, maize and lemongrass have them.  
 Both root systems anchor plants and take up water and dissolved minerals. Their branching patterns differ; their jobs overlap.  
 A taproot can grow deep and reach water below the surface. A deep root system can help a plant through a dry spell, although root depth also depends on the species and the soil.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 15 Many fibrous root systems spread through the upper soil. A dense network helps hold loose soil together and take up water near the surface. Some fibrous roots also reach deep into the ground.  
 A Pattern Appears  
 You now know two ways to sort plants. One uses leaves. One uses roots.  
 Can a record of leaf venation help you predict root type? First collect observations, then test any pattern against another plant.  
 Investigate 1. With your teacher or gardener, select five kinds of flowering plants with developed leaves and visible roots. Use spare nursery plants, not plants pulled from the wild.  2. Make a notebook table using the headings in Table 2.4. Examine four kinds first and record their venation and root type. Mark unclear features as uncertain.  3. Look for a connection in these four records. Use it to predict the root type of the fifth kind from its leaf. Record the prediction before examining its roots.  4. Check the roots of the fifth kind. Does this new observation support your proposed pattern? Compare results across the class.  5. Handle the roots gently and replant the plants with your teacher’s help.  
 Table 2.4 · Leaf venation and root type Plant  Venation  Root prediction (fifth plant)  Root observed  Lemongrass  Parallel  —  Fibrous  Leaf veins. Leaf veins.

CHAPTER 2 Diversity in the Living World LEARNLAB · SCIENCE 6 16 What happened with the fifth plant? An unclear root or leaf is a reason to examine it again, not to change the record so it fits.  
 The Two Go Together  
 Pool the class records. Count how many support a connection and how many do not. Compare the result with these common patterns in flowering plants.  
 Many familiar flowering plants with reticulate venation develop taproots; those with parallel venation commonly develop fibrous root systems.  
 Sadabahar  has net-like veins and a taproot. Chana has net-like veins and a taproot. Lemongrass has parallel veins and fibrous roots. Wheat has parallel veins and fibrous roots.

 The place where a living thing lives is called its  habitat .  
 A habitat includes the conditions and resources an organism uses. Plants need light, water and minerals; animals need food as well as suitable conditions. A habitat need not be safe at all times, and an animal may use different places to feed or breed.

 Case 1 — The sailors' disease  
 On long sea voyages in earlier centuries, sailors fell ill in a particular way. Their gums swelled and bled, their teeth loosened, old wounds reopened, and many died — often months from any battle or storm.  sailing ship 
 In May 1747, James Lind compared six treatments among twelve sailors with scurvy, two sailors per treatment. The pair receiving oranges and lemons improved most rapidly.

 3.4 Cooking, Roughage and Water  
 Have you noticed that a raw carrot snaps and a boiled one bends? That spinach loses its bright green in the pan?  
 Heat changes food, and not only in ways we can see. Some nutrients — Vitamin C among them — are partly destroyed by high heat. Washing vegetables and fruit after cutting or peeling them washes some vitamins away as well.  
 Two sensible conclusions follow. First, include some fruit and raw vegetables in your diet so that not everything you eat has been through a hot pan. Second, wash produce before you cut it, not after.  
 But do wash it. Thoroughly, every time. The vitamins lost to washing are a small price against the dirt, pesticide residue and germs that washing removes.

What sets them apart is what comes with the carbohydrate: substantially more dietary fibre than polished rice, along with iron, calcium and B vitamins.  Long ago, ships sailed from the coast of Kerala carrying pepper, cardamom and ginger. They went to lands far across the sea.  
 Those sailing ships had no engines, and finding a course across open water was difficult. So how did a sailor know which way to go?  
 By day, he watched the sun. By night, he watched the stars. Sailors learnt the night sky so well that they could tell their direction from it.  
 But now think about a storm. Thick clouds cover the sky for two days. There is no sun. There are no stars. There is water in every direction, and every direction looks the same.  
 Which way is home?  
 A naturally magnetic stone, supported so it could turn freely, offered a direction reference when the sky was hidden. A direction alone did not tell sailors their position or the route home.  
 This chapter is about that stone, and about the magnets we use today.

 A hanging magnet works, but it is not much use on a rolling ship. It needs to be small, steady, and easy to read.

 Inside a compass there is a thin magnet shaped like a needle. The needle sits balanced on a sharp pin, so it can turn very easily. Under the needle is a dial with the directions marked on it. A clear cover keeps out wind and rain.  
 Leave the compass on a flat surface and wait. The needle swings and then settles along the north-south line, just as the hanging magnet did. The end that points north is usually painted red, or marked in some other way.

 This small device changed the world. With a compass, a ship could hold its course through cloud, fog and night. It supplied a direction reference; sailors still needed information about their position and planned route.  A freely suspended bar magnet. A freely suspended bar magnet.

CHAPTER 12 Beyond Earth When a comet is warmed by the Sun, some ice changes directly into gas, releasing dust. This forms a surrounding  coma . Sunlight and the solar wind push material generally away from the Sun, forming tails. A tail is not a trail of fire, and it does not simply point backwards along the comet’s path. 
 Some comets return periodically; others may escape, break apart or collide with another body. Halley’s comet takes roughly 76 years per orbit and last passed through the inner Solar System in 1986. A comet’s appearance is a natural event, not evidence that it causes good or bad luck. 
 12.4 Our Home Galaxy 
 From a sufficiently dark location, part of the Milky Way can appear as a faint band across the sky. Its position and visibility depend on season, time and location; it is not always a fixed north-to-south stripe. We see this band because we look through many stars and clouds within our galaxy’s disc. 
 Fig. 12.11 · Artist’s external view of a spiral galaxy. We cannot take this outside view of our own galaxy from Earth. 
 A  galaxy  is an enormous system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. The  Milky   Way   Galaxy , also called Akasha Ganga, is our home galaxy.
